provisioning:Gruž Market.name: Gruž Market
provisioning:Gruž Market.teaser: Walk the fish hall before seven, then the produce stalls outside: a galley's week in two passes
provisioning:Gruž Market.story: Shop it in two passes. Inside the fish hall, decide the menu by what the boats brought: scorpionfish for a brodet, bream to grill whole, a monkfish tail, the morning's octopus for salad. Outside, fill the bag with tomatoes, figs, herbs and a mandolin of homemade olive oil. Carry small notes, because most stalls take only cash.
provisioning:Gruž Market.why: Let the fish decide the menu: buy first in the hall, plan dinner afterwards.
facts: Scorpionfish, sea bream, monkfish and octopus in the fish hall; tomatoes, figs, herbs and olive oil at the outdoor stalls
Early: boats land about 06:30 and the fish is gone by about 10:00; Monday is quiet (seen May 2026)
Cash only at most stalls; bring small notes

provisioning:Gundulić Square market.name: Gundulić Square market
provisioning:Gundulić Square market.teaser: A morning of stalls under the poet's statue: candied orange peel, dried figs and lavender
provisioning:Gundulić Square market.story: Under the bronze of the poet Ivan Gundulić, cast by Ivan Rendić and unveiled in May 1893, a handful of stalls set up each morning and are packing away by about midday. It is smaller and more touristed than Gruž, with little or no fish, but it is the place for things that travel: arancini, the Dubrovnik confection of candied bitter-orange peel, dried figs, lavender bags from Hvar, bunches of herbs, honey and home-made rakija in reused bottles. The reliefs around the plinth show scenes from Gundulić's epic Osman.
provisioning:Gundulić Square market.why: Buy the arancini here: the candied bitter-orange peel is the one Dubrovnik sweet that keeps for weeks on board.
facts: Most mornings; some guides say Monday to Saturday, others daily (check on Sunday)
From about 07:00 to around midday (Oct 2026 listings disagree)
Before 10:00, ahead of the walking tours
Arancini (candied bitter-orange peel), dried figs, Hvar lavender, honey, herbs, olive oil in glass bottles

provisioning:The oyster quay at Mali Sto.name: The oyster quay at Mali Ston
provisioning:The oyster quay at Mali Sto.teaser: Buy from the growers themselves at Mali Ston: bring ice and a cool box, and ring ahead out of season
provisioning:The oyster quay at Mali Sto.story: Taking oysters back to the galley is a matter of logistics. Bring a cool box, ice and cash in small notes. Through the busy months the growers' boats tie up at the Mali Ston waterfront and sell oysters and mussels straight from the bay. By late October the quay is quiet, so do not count on finding someone there. Telephone a grower or Bota Šare the day before and arrange a pick-up. Several farms, at Mali Ston, Zamaslina, Hodilje and Luka, also take visitors out to the beds by boat. Keep the oysters cold, cupped side down, and open them on board.
provisioning:The oyster quay at Mali Sto.why: Arrange the pick-up the day before: in late autumn the quay sells only to those who have rung ahead.
facts: In season, most mornings at the quay; from late October, by arrangement with a grower
Before lunch, so the oysters are on ice for the drive back

provisioning:Grgić Vina.name: Grgić Vina
provisioning:Grgić Vina.teaser: A cellar door at Trstenik with exactly two wines: carry both back to the boat
provisioning:Grgić Vina.story: Choosing is easy here, because the cellar makes only two wines: a white, Pošip, and a red, Plavac Mali. Taste both, then take bottles of each back to the boat, the Pošip for the fish and the Plavac for the lamb or the peka. Visits are small and by appointment, so email at least a week ahead. Come late morning, then drive on to oysters at Mali Ston.
provisioning:Grgić Vina.why: The Pošip is the bottle to buy for the galley: dry, salty and made to be drunk with the day's fish.
facts: Pošip Grgić and Plavac Mali Grgić, the only two wines
Email at least a week ahead; +385 20 748 090
Tasting about EUR 25-45 per person (seen May 2026)

provisioning:Saints Hills.name: Saints Hills
provisioning:Saints Hills.teaser: An abandoned stone winery at Oskorušno, revived by the Tolj family, pours its reds on the roof
provisioning:Saints Hills.story: The cellar house at Oskorušno had been a working winery until its owners left for overseas. It then stood empty for about eighty years, until the Tolj family restored it as Vinaria, the Pelješac home of Saints Hills, an estate with Michel Rolland as consultant. Sommeliers pour three to five wines, with a plate of Pag cheese or prosciutto if you want one. The reds are served on the roof terrace above the vines. Of the two flagship Plavac Malis, Sveta Lucija comes from the Dingač slopes and Sveti Roko from Komarna, across the channel. There is an Istrian white too, the Malvazija called Nevina.
provisioning:Saints Hills.why: Taste the two Plavacs side by side: Dingač and Komarna show how much the slope changes the grape.
facts: Vinaria, Oskorušno, on the Pelješac peninsula road
Tastings by booking; winery tours at 13:00, 15:00 and 19:00 (Oct 2026 booking listing); check the season
Sveta Lucija (Dingač), Sveti Roko (Komarna), Nevina Malvazija
Tasting flights of three, four or five wines; check the current price when booking

provisioning:Uje.name: Uje
provisioning:Uje.teaser: A Croatian olive-oil shop on the Stradun: Korčula and Konavle oils in bottles that travel
provisioning:Uje.story: Uje means oil in Dalmatian dialect, and the shop sells little else that does not belong next to it. On the shelves are oils from Croatian estates in Istria and Dalmatia, beside jars of pickled capers, jams, honey and small bottles of rakija. Go past the famous Istrian names to the smaller Dalmatian oils from Korčula and Konavle, which are less often seen abroad. A box of Ston sea-salt flakes travels well in the same bag.
provisioning:Uje.why: Ask to taste a Korčula oil next to an Istrian one before buying: the difference is the reason to come.
facts: Old Town, a shopfront facing the Stradun; another Dubrovnik branch is listed at Zamanjina 1 (Oct 2026 listings)

provisioning:The Franciscan pharmacy.name: The Franciscan pharmacy
provisioning:The Franciscan pharmacy.teaser: Friars have dispensed medicine inside Pile Gate since 1317: buy the rose cream, see the old jars
provisioning:The Franciscan pharmacy.story: The Friars Minor opened their pharmacy in 1317, and it has dispensed medicine ever since, now from a counter just inside Pile Gate. It was among the first in Europe to serve the general public, not only the monks. What a visitor takes away is the creams, made from local plants to the friars' old formulas: rose cream, almond oil, lavender and pine balms. Painted jars, mortars and ledgers from the early apothecary sit in the monastery museum off the Romanesque cloister.
provisioning:The Franciscan pharmacy.why: Buy a jar of the rose cream: it is made to an old Franciscan formula and fits in a crew bag.
facts: Franciscan Monastery, Placa 2, just inside Pile Gate
About 09:00-18:00 in summer; winter hours reported as 09:00-17:00 or 09:00-14:00 (check)

provisioning:Asia Shop.name: Asia Shop
provisioning:Asia Shop.teaser: Need nori or mirin for a guest? Ring this Lapad grocer before you send the tender
provisioning:Asia Shop.story: Treat this one as a phone number before an address. The old guide sends a galley's Japanese or Thai request to a small Asian grocer in Lapad, on Iva Vojnovića. On that list are soy sauce and mirin, sushi rice and nori, rice vinegars, gochujang, Thai curry pastes and kecap manis. Its stock changes, and we could not confirm in October 2026 that it still trades. Call ahead with a list before anyone makes the trip.
provisioning:Asia Shop.why: Call with the exact list first: the stock changes, and the shop's 2026 trading is unconfirmed.

provisioning:Konzum by Pile Gate.name: Konzum on Gundulić Square
provisioning:Konzum by Pile Gate.teaser: The supermarket inside the walls, where water costs what it costs in Gruž, not on the Stradun
provisioning:Konzum by Pile Gate.story: The Konzum inside the walls is where people who still live in the Old Town do their shopping. It stands by Gundulić Square, a few steps from the morning stalls. Buy the cases of water here rather than at the Stradun cafés, which charge several times as much. There are also Croatian staples: the Podravka shelf, Vegeta for a Balkan stew, and Dolcela mixes for a quick galley cake.
provisioning:Konzum by Pile Gate.why: Buy water and pantry staples here: inside the walls nothing else is priced like a neighbourhood shop.
facts: Gundulićeva poljana 11, Old Town (inside the walls, not outside Pile Gate)
Check the hours at the store

walks:The city walls.name: The city walls
walks:The city walls.teaser: A one-way walk of 1,940 m round the rooftops, from the Pile bastions to Minčeta and back to the gate
walks:The city walls.story: Climb from Pile Gate past Bokar, Michelozzo's two-storey casemate of 1461-63, and follow the sea wall east above the rocks, the swell sounding below, terracotta roofs and washing lines. The ring turns north round the harbour and up to Minčeta, the round tower of 1464 by Michelozzo and Juraj Dalmatinac: at 25 m the highest point. Across the cove Lovrijenac sits on its own 37 m rock, its seaward walls 12 m thick, its city-facing ones 60 cm, so the city could bring it down if it were ever lost. Over its door: Non bene pro toto libertas venditur auro. Your ticket covers it; Hamlet plays there in summer.
walks:The city walls.why: From Minčeta you see the whole Stradun from above, the view that explains how the city is laid out.
facts: Pile Gate; adult ticket about EUR 40, including Fort Lovrijenac within three days, with a lower winter rate reported (Oct 2026, unofficial listings)
Stone walkways and steep steps; no shade on the second half
At opening or late afternoon; from November to March about 09:00-15:00 (Oct 2026 listings)
The view from Minčeta, and Lovrijenac with its inscription
Water, a hat and shoes with grip: the stone gets very hot in full sun

walks:Stradun and the five squares.name: Stradun and the five squares
walks:Stradun and the five squares.teaser: From Onofrio's fountain to the Jesuit stairs: the Old Town in five squares, best before nine
walks:Stradun and the five squares.story: Start at Pile with Onofrio's great fountain of 1438. The water once came from a spring 12 km away, and it still pours from sixteen stone masks. Walk the Stradun's 300 m of limestone, worn smooth as glass, to Luža Square. Here are the small Onofrio fountain, St Blaise's Church, the bell tower and Orlando's Column of 1418, from which decrees were once read out. Turn right for Gundulić Square and its morning stalls, then climb the Baroque Jesuit stairs to St Ignatius on Poljana Boškovića. Finish on Bunićeva poljana by the cathedral, a few steps from the Old Port.
walks:Stradun and the five squares.why: Climb the Jesuit stairs before nine, when the square at the top is still empty.
facts: Onofrio's great fountain, just inside Pile Gate
Flat polished limestone, then steps; slippery in rain

walks:Mount Srđ and Fort Imperial.name: Mount Srđ and Fort Imperial
walks:Mount Srđ and Fort Imperial.teaser: A few minutes by cable car from above the walls to a Napoleonic fort with the whole coast below
walks:Mount Srđ and Fort Imperial.story: The cable car lifts you from above Buža Gate to the summit of Srđ, about 412 m above the sea, in a few minutes. At the top the Old Town looks like a model, with Lokrum and the Elaphiti out to sea. Napoleon's French built Fort Imperial here, finishing it in 1812. It now holds the museum of Dubrovnik in the Homeland War, telling the 1991-92 siege from the hill the defenders held. Bring a jacket: the bora blows harder up here. For the walk down there is a zigzag footpath with Stations of the Cross.
walks:Mount Srđ and Fort Imperial.why: Go up in the late afternoon and come down on foot, with the Old Town below you the whole way.
facts: Cable car lower station, above Buža Gate
About 412 m of height, cable car or footpath
Half a day with the museum

walks:The walls of Ston.name: The walls of Ston
walks:The walls of Ston.teaser: The Republic walled a whole isthmus to guard its salt: climb from Ston over the hill to Mali Ston
walks:The walls of Ston.story: Ston came under Dubrovnik in 1333, and the Republic set out to wall off the whole isthmus of Pelješac. Between the two towns the walls climb over a steep hill, linking Ston's walls on the salt-pan side with Mali Ston on the bay. Climb the stepped ramparts to the high towers and you look down on the square ponds of the Ston salt pans on one side and the oyster lines of the bay on the other. On a still day you can hear the gulls from both. Coming down to Mali Ston you arrive at the oyster tables of Bota Šare.
walks:The walls of Ston.why: From the top tower you can see why the walls were built: salt on one side, the sea on the other.
facts: The wall entrance in Ston, by the salt pans

walks:The Ljuta and its mills.name: The Ljuta and its mills
walks:The Ljuta and its mills.teaser: A cold spring river in Konavle that turned the Republic's millstones: walk upstream past them
walks:The Ljuta and its mills.story: Konavle was the Republic's grain field, and the Ljuta ground its flour. Along this short spring-fed river there were once eight flour mills, two oil mills and three fulling mills for cloth, fed by channels and three small aqueducts. Walk upstream from the village beside the water. It runs clear and fast, and the air beside the channels is cooler than the valley. One mill still turns and grinds flour, and the source and the upper river are protected. Afterwards, lunch at Konoba Konavoski Dvori, by the water.
walks:The Ljuta and its mills.why: Go in autumn, when there is enough water in the river to turn the wheels.
facts: Ljuta village, by Konoba Konavoski Dvori, about 35 minutes' drive south-east of Dubrovnik
